title: Work and study
goal: Talk about jobs and ambitions with two endings you haven't used yet, and build sentences that don't say who does the action — the form found on every Finnish notice board.
bekal: talk about your job, education and work plans

notes: **Olin tarjoilijana** — the ending **-na/-nä** means "as", and it's the ending used for a job you're doing or used to do. You already know it from the days of the week (*maanantaina*) and from *ensimmäisenä* in unit 13; this is its third use.

**Opiskelen insinööriksi** — the ending **-ksi** means "becoming". It's used for a change of state: studying **to become** an engineer, wanting **to become** a doctor. So *-na* and *-ksi* pair up like "as" and "becoming" — one is a current state, the other the goal of a change.

**Suomea puhutaan täällä** — a sentence without a subject. It doesn't say who speaks; what matters is the action. English uses the passive: "Finnish **is spoken** here". Both languages are comfortable dropping the doer, but Finnish does it far more often, even in casual speech.

**Otetaan sinut** — the same form is used for suggestions ("let's") and for subjectless sentences ("is taken"). Only the situation tells them apart. *Mennään!* = let's go; *Suomessa mennään saunaan* = in Finland people go to the sauna.

**Pidän kiireestä** — *pitää* with the "from" ending means "to like". Note that this is the same verb as *pitää* for obligation in unit 17; what differs is the structure. *Pidän kahvi**sta*** = I like coffee.
**Täydellistä, harvinaista** — partial forms again for judging uncountable things. The same pattern as *hienoa*, *kallista*, *erinomaista*, which have been scattered around since unit 6.

grammars.title: As (-na) and becoming (-ksi)
body: Two endings that pair up and are very useful, and both are used far more widely than just for jobs.

after: **Language names take -ksi** to mean "in (language)": *suomeksi*, *englanniksi*, *indonesiaksi*. This is the use you'll need most often: *Mitä tämä on suomeksi?* (what's this in Finnish?).

*Olen opettaja* and *olen opettajana* are both correct but slightly different: the first states your identity, the second what you're doing at the moment. If you're a trained teacher now working in a café: *olen opettaja, mutta olen tällä hetkellä tarjoilijana*.
⚠️ Gradation applies as usual: *opettaja → opettajana* (no change), but *lapsi → lapsena*, *kuukausi → kuukaudeksi*.

grammars.title: Sentences without a subject
body: A form that doesn't say who's doing the action. It's on every notice board, in every rule and in every casual suggestion in Finland — and there's only one form, which doesn't change for anyone.

head: Verb
Subjectless
Example
Meaning
rows: In Finland people eat a lot of fish.

after: **Two jobs, one form.** With an exclamation mark or an inviting tone, it means "let's". As part of a statement, it's a passive with no doer. Finns never confuse the two, and after a few weeks neither will you.
**Negating it:** *ei puhuta*, *ei mennä*, *ei syödä*, *ei saa*. Notice the form gets shorter — just like ordinary negatives drop the ending.
⚠️ For now, learn the forms in the table as they are. Forming them from any verb is a bit tricky and belongs to A2; the ones above already cover almost everything you need.

blocks.text: Notice that almost all of them end in **-ja/-jä**, meaning "person who does" — formed from the verb, much like English *-er*: *opettaa* (teach) → *opettaja*, *myydä* (sell) → *myyjä*, *tarjoilla* (serve) → *tarjoilija*. If you know the verb, you can guess the job.

head: Suomi

blocks.title: What's really required
items: For tech and research jobs in Helsinki, English is often enough. For almost any job dealing with people — cafés, shops, care work, education — Finnish is **a must**.

The levels job ads usually ask for: *sujuva suomi* (fluent) or *hyvä suomen kielen taito* (good command). The equivalent of this A1 is *suomen kielen alkeet* — and that's already enough to show commitment, which often matters more than the level itself.
Being honest about your skills actually helps: *Puhun vähän suomea, mutta opiskelen aktiivisesti.* Exaggerating will be obvious within two minutes.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Finnish job interviews are much flatter in tone than many people expect: little small talk, little praise, lots of direct questions. A brief silence after a question is seen as a sign you're thinking, not that you're unprepared. Don't fill it.
